tip: Ordering: thing + 주세요: 물 주세요 (mul juseyo = water, please). A fixed phrase — use it as is.
좀 softens a request: 김치 좀 주세요 (gimchi jom juseyo = some kimchi, please).
Korean asks 'where is X' through the exist verb: 화장실이 어디에 있어요? (hwajangsil-i eodi-e isseoyo?) is literally 'bathroom where exists?'
Korean splits 'there' in two: 여기 (yeogi = here), 거기 (geogi = there by you), 저기 (jeogi = over there). 여기에 있어요 (yeogi-e isseoyo) = it's here.
In 'where is X?' questions X takes 이/가 (i/ga): 지하철역이 어디에 있어요? (jihacheollyeok-i eodi-e isseoyo?) – 이/가 presents it as new to the conversation.

english: The hospital is next to the school.
tip: Location words follow their noun: 학교 옆에 (hakgyo yeop-e) is literally 'school beside-at' – the reverse of English 'next to the school'.

english: The café is in front of the bank.
tip: Position words come after their noun: 은행 앞에 (eunhaeng ap-e, literally 'bank front-at') – the reverse of English 'in front of the bank'.
Korean has a single verb for 'is not there': 없어요 (eopseoyo). 열쇠가 여기에 없어요 (yeolsoe-ga yeogi-e eopseoyo = the key isn't here) – no 'is' + 'not' combo.
Just being somewhere takes 에 (e): 집에 있어요 (jib-e isseoyo = is at home). Save 에서 (eseo) for places where an action happens.
Korean adjectives work like verbs — no 'is' needed: 좋아요 (joayo) alone means 'it's good'.
맛있어요 (masisseoyo = delicious) is literally 'taste exists': 맛 (mat = taste) + 있어요 (isseoyo = there is). So 불고기가 맛있어요 (bulgogi-ga masisseoyo) = the bulgogi has taste.
너무 (neomu) is literally 'too (much)', but everyday speech also uses it for plain 'so': 너무 비싸요 (neomu bissayo) can be a real complaint or just emphasis.
Koreans say 우리 집 (uri jip = our house) even for a home they live in alone – 우리 (uri) covers home, family, and country. 제 집 (je jip = my house) sounds oddly distant.

english: The airport is far from home.
tip: 에서 also means 'from' with distance: 집에서 멀어요 (jib-eseo meoreoyo = far from home).
Day words take no particle: 어제 뭐 했어요? (eoje mwo haesseoyo = what did you do yesterday?) – but parts of the day do: 아침에 (achime = in the morning).
만나다 takes 을/를, not 'with': 친구를 만났어요 (chingureul mannasseoyo = met a friend).
있다 (itda = to be somewhere) takes 에 (e), not 에서 (eseo): 집에 있었어요 (jibe isseosseoyo = I was at home).
는 after a time word adds contrast: 어제는 (eojeneun = as for yesterday).
아침 (achim) means both morning and breakfast: 아침을 먹다 (achimeul meokda) is literally 'eat the morning'. Context decides which one you mean.

english: I was late for work today.
tip: 늦다 takes 에 for what you are late to: 회사에 늦었어요 (hoesae neujeosseoyo = was late for work).

english: On Sunday I got up late.
tip: Adverbs sit right before the verb: 늦게 일어났어요 (neutge ireonasseoyo) is literally 'late got-up' – English tacks 'late' on at the end instead.
Korean 'shoots' photos: 사진을 찍어요 (sajineul jjigeoyo = take a photo).

english: On Friday evening I ate fried chicken.
tip: The loanword 치킨 (chikin) narrowed to fried chicken only – chicken as meat in cooking is 닭고기 (dakgogi).
저녁 (jeonyeok) means both evening and dinner: 저녁을 안 먹었어요 (jeonyeogeul an meogeosseoyo = didn't eat dinner) – 점심 (jeomsim) likewise covers midday and lunch.

english: I ate bibimbap at a restaurant.
tip: 에서 (eseo) marks where an action happens: 식당에서 비빔밥을 먹었어요 (sikdangeseo bibimbabeul meogeosseoyo = ate bibimbap at a restaurant) – 에 (e) would mark a destination instead.

english: I ate samgyeopsal with a friend.
tip: 랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with': 친구랑 (chingurang = with a friend). In writing or formal speech, 하고 (hago) or 와/과 (wa/gwa) fit better.

english: I drank a lot of water.
tip: 많이 (mani = a lot) goes before the verb: 많이 마셨어요 = drank a lot.
뭐 샀어요? (mwo sasseoyo = what did you buy?) — 뭐 usually drops its particle in speech.
Korean adjectives take past endings like verbs: 비쌌어요 (bissasseoyo = was expensive).
쓰다 means write, use, AND spend: 돈을 다 썼어요 (doneul da sseosseoyo = spent all the money).
